record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: Are there words all of whose prefixes have palindromic length at most n but some factor has palindromic length 2n?

evidence.quote: Are there words such that all of their prefixes have palindromic length at most n, but some of their factors have palindromic length 2n?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A word $w \in A^*$ is a palindrome if it equals its reversal. The palindromic length of a word $w$, denoted $\mathrm{PL}(w)$, is the least integer $k \geq 0$ such that $w$ can be written as a concatenation $w = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$ of palindromes $p_i \in A^*$ (with $\mathrm{PL}(\varepsilon) = 0$). For an infinite word $\mathbf{w} = w_1 w_2 w_3 \cdots$ over $A$, a prefix is any word of the form $w_1 \cdots w_m$ ($m \geq 0$), and a factor is any word of the form $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_j$ ($1 \leq i \leq j+1$).

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $n$ and an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ (or a finite word) such that every prefix of $\mathbf{w}$ has palindromic length at most $n$, yet some factor of $\mathbf{w}$ has palindromic length equal to $2n$?

Equivalently, is the bound $\mathrm{PL}(\text{factor}) \leq 2n$ — given that all prefixes satisfy $\mathrm{PL}(\text{prefix}) \leq n$ — tight, or can it always be improved?
artifact.status_search_result: Saarela established that if every prefix of a word is a product of at most n palindromes, then every factor is a product of at most 2n palindromes, showing the 2n bound. Whether this bound is attained — i.e., whether there exist words with prefix palindromic length at most n but some factor of palindromic length exactly 2n — does not appear to be settled in the available literature, so the tightness question is recorded as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Palindromic Length in Free Monoids and Free Groups
status_evidence.snippet: Saarela proved that if every prefix of a word is a product of n palindromes, then every factor is a product of 2n palindromes.
status_evidence.claim: The factor palindromic length is at most twice the prefix palindromic length bound, but the tightness (existence of factors achieving exactly 2n) is not resolved.

status_evidence.title: On prefix palindromic length of automatic words
status_evidence.snippet: The conjecture that prefix palindromic length is unbounded for every non-ultimately-periodic infinite word remains open in general.
status_evidence.claim: Related palindromic length problems remain active and only partially solved.
